notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on John 3. I ran out of searches before covering every verse, so some verses are missing or thin, and several of the sources you listed aren't here. The gaps are listed at the end.

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Nicodemus was a member of the ruling Sanhedrin. He was religious, educated and influential. Guzik sees him as standing for the best in humanity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- Precept Austin passes on a Jewish tradition that he was the third richest man in Jerusalem at this time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik thinks Nicodemus may have come at night because he was timid, or because he wanted to talk without interruption. Guzik also notes that his reasoning from miracles was not entirely sound, since false prophets can perform signs too (2 Thess 2:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- Bob Utley (quoted by Precept Austin) says calling Jesus a teacher from God was true but not enough. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary

**v. 3**
- **The Greek word.** *Anothen* can mean "again" or "from above." Guzik says the meaning is much the same either way, and quotes Morris that both senses are probably intended. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- **A different view.** Calvin rejected "from above." He reasoned that Jesus was speaking Hebrew, which would not have had the same ambiguity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-3.html
- **What Jesus was challenging.** D. A. Carson (quoted by Precept Austin) says most Jews of the time assumed every Jew would enter the kingdom, apart from apostates or the very wicked. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary
- Gill makes the same point: the nation assumed that being descended from Abraham was enough. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-3.html
- Guzik says moral or religious reform is not enough. A person can wash himself, but he cannot give birth to himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/

**v. 4**
- **Nicodemus misunderstood.** The bible.org commentary says he took Jesus too literally and thought of a second physical birth. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-3
- **Readings of his question differ.** Precept Austin collects several:
  - Merrill Tenney: Nicodemus meant "I'm too old to change."
  - Charles Swindoll: he may have been stretching the image on purpose, as a debating move.
  - D. A. Carson: he was genuinely puzzled.
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary
- Guzik quotes Dods: Nicodemus would have understood if Jesus had said every *Gentile* must be born again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/

**v. 5 (the main point of disagreement)**
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel)** lists five readings of "water": baptism, physical birth, the Word, the Spirit, and the cleansing promised in Ezekiel 36:25–28. He finds Ezekiel the strongest, though "a tough call." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- **Reformed (Ligonier).** Jesus was almost certainly not referring specifically to Christian baptism. Even so, the Westminster Confession was right to cite the verse, because Scripture often links water imagery with new birth. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/baptism-and-regeneration
- **Barnes (Presbyterian).** By "water," here, is evidently signified "baptism." He treats it as the sign and seal of the renewing influences of his Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wnt/john/3-5.html
- **Early Methodist teaching.** An 1825 Methodist Episcopal edition of the Doctrinal Tracts, quoted on StudyLight, says By water, then, as a means, the water of baptism, we are regenerated or born again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-5.html
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist)** says the water was only an emblem of the Holy Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wnt/john/3-5.html
- **Restoration Movement.** B. W. Johnson takes "born of water" to mean baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-5.html
- **Sam Storms (charismatic, Reformed).** He describes three baptism-based views:
  - Roman Catholic: baptism always works regeneration (*ex opere operato*).
  - A middle view: the Spirit regenerates, but through baptism.
  - Baptism as the outward sign of an inner new birth.
  
  He argues against all three. The wind image in verse 8 shows the Spirit acting freely, which would be a highly inappropriate analogy if regeneration is inextricably tied to water baptism. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/john-3:5---part-i
- **GotQuestions (evangelical).** The water is not literal (neither baptism nor the womb). It stands for the Spirit's inner cleansing. https://www.gotquestions.org/baptism-John-3-5.html
- **J. Vernon McGee** takes the water to be the Word of God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/regeneration-new-birth
- **Constable** notes that the Greek has no article before "Spirit," so a literal rendering is "born of water and spirit." https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary
- **Catholic.** Catholic.com calls John 3:5 a key text on rebirth. It quotes Justin Martyr, who says converts are brought to water and regenerated there. https://www.catholic.com/tract/born-again-in-baptism

**v. 6**
- Matthew Henry: our corrupt nature comes from our first birth, so the new nature must come from a second birth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_003.cfm
- Alford (quoted by Guzik): "flesh" includes a person's spirit, which is dead in sin from natural birth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/

**v. 7**
- Precept Austin notes that "you" changes from singular to plural here, so the need applies to everyone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary
- Morris (quoted by Guzik): these words rule out salvation by human merit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/

**v. 8**
- Guzik: we don't understand the wind, but we see what it does. In the same way, Nicodemus didn't need to understand the new birth fully before experiencing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- William Kelly stresses the Spirit's sovereign, uncontrolled work. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-1.html

**vv. 9–10**
- Guzik: Jesus rebuked Nicodemus because the Old Testament plainly taught the new birth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- The bible.org commentary agrees that the Old Testament gave Nicodemus enough to understand. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-3

**vv. 12–13**
- In the bible.org commentary, "earthly things" means what Jesus had just said, including the need for new birth. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-3
- Guzik quotes Morris: only Jesus can speak with authority about heaven. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the bronze serpent of Numbers 21 pictures the Messiah. He quotes F. F. Bruce that Jesus now made the point with a story Nicodemus had known since childhood. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- Chuck Smith: being born again is possible only because the Son of Man was crucified. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/c2000_Jhn/Jhn_003.cfm

**v. 16 (Calvinist and Arminian readings of "world")**
- **Guzik:** verse 7 overturned the popular idea of the *way* to salvation; verse 16 overturns the popular idea of its *scope*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-3/
- **Ligonier (Reformed)** sets out three views: everyone without exception, the elect only, and Warfield's view. It prefers Warfield, who says "world" describes how great God's love is (not here a term of extension so much as a term of intensity) rather than how many it covers. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/articles/what-does-world-mean-john-316
- **Monergism (Reformed):** the verse speaks of the breadth of God's love beyond Israel, not of how people come to believe. https://www.monergism.com/does-john-316-refute-calvinism
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Jesus was sent for everyone in the sense that whoever believes in him should not perish. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/what-we-believe-about-the-five-points-of-calvinism
- **A. W. Pink** argues against reading "world" as everyone. https://www.monergism.com/meaning-%E2%80%9Ckosmos%E2%80%9D-john-316
- **Barnes:** "world" means all mankind, and he cites Hebrews 2:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-16.html
- **Clarke (Wesleyan):** God gave his Son to die for the world, but only those who believe are saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-16.html
- **Steven Cole (bible.org)** thinks both sides go wrong. Some Calvinists limit "world" to the elect; some Arminians deny God's special, electing love. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-17-god-s-shocking-love-john-316-18

**v. 19**
- John Hendryx (Monergism) uses this verse to qualify verse 16: the offer goes to all, but people love the darkness. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/world316.html

**vv. 25–30**
- Craig Evans (quoted by Precept Austin): if some early readers set John up as Jesus' rival, this passage corrects that. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary

**v. 27**
- Precept Austin reads this verse as a statement of sovereign grace. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary

**v. 29**
- Barclay: Israel was pictured as God's bride, and John took the role of the bridegroom's friend. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-22.html
- Matthew Henry applies this to ministers, who are friends of the bridegroom. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-22.html
- Sproul: John did not want the bride; he was glad to stand with Christ. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/jesus-john-baptist

**v. 30**
- William MacDonald (quoted by Precept Austin): this verse sums up John's ministry. A servant who draws attention to himself is being disloyal. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john_330_commentary

**v. 31**
- Craig Evans links this verse's *anothen* ("from above") to the same word in verse 3. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-3-commentary

**vv. 33–34**
- Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org): rejecting Jesus' words is calling God a liar. https://bible.org/seriespage/john%E2%80%99s-joy-and-his-disciples%E2%80%99-jealousy-john-322-36
- Matthew Henry: the prophets had the Spirit in measure; Christ had him without measure. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-22.html
- William Kelly reads it differently: God also gives the Spirit without measure *through* Jesus to others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-22.html

**v. 35**
- Sproul: God's love for us rests on his eternal love for the Son. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/jesus-john-baptist

**v. 36**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "abides" means the wrath is on the unbeliever now. He also argues this rules out annihilation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-36.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God's wrath is active displeasure, not just "the consuming fire of infinite love." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-36.html
- **Barclay, by contrast:** a person brings wrath on himself rather than God sending it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/3-22.html
- **Translation:** versions differ between "does not believe" and "does not obey." https://biblehub.com/parallel/john/3-36.htm

**What's missing**
- **Verses with no notes:** 11, 15, 17–18, 20–24, 26, 28 and 32.
- **Sources not reached:**
  - NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey
  - Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org)
  - Orthodox commentary (oca.org only gave the bare text) and New Advent
  - Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary on most verses
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.
